title: Free jazz on the Lower East Side and Bartok synthesis
summary: Free players had tiny audiences at first; the music incubated in two Lower East Side spots including Slug's, later synthesized into the mainstream, as with Bartok.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Okay. I wonder if you have ever attended a concert, let’s say someone like Albert Ayler who was on the far end of where things could go, and witnessed a reaction like the audience at the premier of “The Rite of Spring”?

Well you know those fellows, when they were creating that free form thing, and I watched that because I broke in right at the same time, there wasn’t an audience really. There was like a few family and friends. And you know the writers in the magazines gave it a big lift you know. And then people started to say well what is this all about, and started to come. And there were two places on the Lower East Side where this was incubated and really got going. And one was called a speakeasy. Actually that place is still there, I mean the location of it, where these guys would go and work on this. And there was a place called Slug’s, a little bit farther east on the Lower East Side of Manhattan, in what we call Alphabet City, you know, Avenue A, B, C, and D. And there it started to really get legs you know in those places. And the rest is history with that too I

mean for the beboppers, so-called straight ahead guys, you know some of it got incorporated into, you know, the mainstream of things. And just like with classical music you know, things got worked out. I mean a perfect example is I mean I guess my all-time favorite classical composer, musician, is Bartok. And the reason why is not only is his works, you know, just out of this world great, but you know he said you know I’m really a Bach guy. You know? But he took that and did like what happened with all our form, with the guys that started there, it got synthesized and worked up into the main body, the quintessential body of the art form. Because Bartok’s earlier work, you can hear that he loved Bach you know? But then when you hear the string quartet it’s unsurpassed. And so you know, then you hear like, who you mentioned, Albert Ayler and Archie Schepp. I mean Archie Schepp actually is not as far out as was Albert Ayler and some of the other guys. Because Archie can go either way, as you know, until today. And all of the, you know my generation that was coming up then it didn’t matter what the instrument, they all synthesized some of that and made it even better, what was being attempted. So that’s my take on it.
